title: Time zones, schedules, and jobs that run twice
outcome: Separate an instant, a local calendar rule, a schedule trigger, and a unique business run.
useCase: Daily reports, reminders, and tenant-local deadlines.
benefits: Prevents common duplicate and off-by-a-day defects.
drawbacks: Calendar changes and ambiguous outcomes need explicit policy.
cue: A time is not a date. A tick is not a completed run.

trace.title: Calendar rule and zone
trace.detail:
## Understand the idea

“Tomorrow at 9” needs a time zone and a calendar rule. Store an instant for an event that already happened.

Store the intended zone/rule as well when scheduling future local-time behavior. Daylight-saving transitions can create missing or repeated local times.

cron or a scheduler triggers work. It does not guarantee exactly one business run.

Two schedulers, retries, or a delayed process can trigger the same logical period more than once. Define a unique run key such as workspace plus report date, backed by a database rule.

A job should load current state, tolerate retry according to its contract, and expose a useful outcome. Passing an ID is usually better than serializing a whole model object.

A scheduled trigger and a durable work record are different things.

trace.title: Follow one item
trace.detail:
Scheduler tick → compute intended business period → claim unique run → snapshot/request work → job retries → durable completion state.

If a process crashes after claiming, define how a stale in-progress run is retried or repaired.

Test a late scheduler, duplicate trigger, a DST boundary, and a provider timeout. “It ran yesterday” is weak evidence for these cases.

trace.title: Try the failure
trace.detail:
A mutex in one Ruby process does not coordinate multiple schedulers. A UTC date and a user-local date can refer to different report periods.

A done flag written before the effect can lose work.
